Some of us are honest about our results. Some of the results are flat out lies, completely made up by ambitious, career-driven, and stressed out students trying to pad their resumes and accepted by trusting primary investigators (PIs) as legitimate observation. Some PIs, themselves, under extreme pressure by their academic department heads and university staff to "publish or perish" are willing to accept false data or even create it themselves in order to get something with positive results they can farm out to a journal.

The journals themselves are businesses. They have a strong bias for "breakthroughs." It's exceedingly rare to see negative results published. Publishing that something didn't work is often critical so we don't waste time replicating a failed avenue of investigation. Then we have the various journals' standards for peer review. Remember that the peers doing the reviewing are paid, and they're paid to put their names and reputations as a stamp on the research and say it's good. It takes tremendous amount of time and effort to really comb through a data set and find errors in methodology, statistical method, or results. I know. My PI on one project was a reviewer who did the hard work, did find errors, and it consumed enormous amounts of her time to go back through software to make sure it properly modeled the manual technique to produce accurate results. So much of our research is dependent on algorithms and computer modeling that this type of validation is indispensible. It also requires highly specialized expertise and a LOT of time to dig, time that could be spent on their own projects and their own publications. There's a lot of incentive to rubber stamp papers and collect the quick paycheck.

Ultimately, (and pay really close attention to this) it has been found that up to ~85% of medical research cannot be replicated! Which means those results which look great on paper and look completely legit, aren't, because human complexity is what it is, and we can't repeat the result. And it's not just small-time work and "student projects." Amgen engaged a team to replicate 53 "landmark clinical trials", the biggest and best of Big Pharma, the studies that form the core of medial practice guidelines used by doctors all over the world. They did it because they wanted to know if they could trust the results in shaping their own future lines of research, a huge, billion-dollar financial incentive to validate and be 100% sure the studies are accurate. [Prinz F, Schlange T, Asadullah K. Believe it or not: how much can we rely on published data on potential drug targets? Nat Rev Drug Discov. 2011;10:712.]

Medical research is an industry, but it's not treated like automobile or aircraft manufacture. There's no six sigma process for a medical study, even at "paper factories" like Vanderbilt, Stanford, Harvard, Duke, etc. And the result is that despite our best intentions and enormous quantities of dollars and time invested, we still make a lot of mistakes - mistakes that get people killed, without us ever being aware of it because we think the data show we're curing people.
